newsitem.title: UK: SUGAR - World market awaits NY expiry for Brazil raw.
newsitem.headline: SUGAR - World market awaits NY expiry for Brazil raw.

text.p: Free-market supply of Brazilian FOB raw sugar from the new centre-south (CS) crop is expected to remain thin on the ground until the July futures expiry, physical brokers said on Friday.

Much of the new-crop CS shipments to date have come out of Paranagua, which became a centre of attention when U.S. trade house Cargill took delivery of 260,000 long tons of raws tendered against May futures.
Brazil's CS harvest traditionally begins in May but most traders agree that Cargill's Brazilian supplier is using new crop sugar and not stocks.
Traders have cited talk that Brazil still has ample stocks from last year's crop, available to be delivered against July or to be released onto the world market.
"The only (CS) raws that are really on the market at the moment are out of the May expiry," said one broker.
But these were not available to the free market as Cargill was shipping them to end-users and so there were no inter-trade quotes, he said.
"I think you'll see most of that (new crop sugars) against the July. It's still quite early for Brazils so they'll probably come out when July expires."

But traders quoted Black Sea C & F cargoes as Brazil moved to satisfy Russian demand in the absence of much supply from other western hemisphere producers such as Mexico and Guatemala -- at the tail-end of their crops.
June arrival cargoes were bid at a $42 premium over July futures with June shipments at $38/46 bid/offer.
"Most people are focussing on the c & f Black Sea market, depending on where they can fix rates. That's probably why there are no quotes on a FOB basis," said one London physical trader.
"With Cargill taking all this stuff out of Paranagua and most people reasonably well loaded out of Santos, there isn't a great deal around to sell on a FOB basis."
But shipments from Santos, Brazil's principal sugar port, in May were very much down on last year.
Provisional figures showed only 6,549 tonnes of bagged sugar shipped while the first bulk ship of the new crop year had only begun loading recently.
In May last year, the port handled 59,723 tonnes of bagged sugar, 27,819 tonnes of bulk and 6,675 tonnes at Cargill's private terminal.

Market sources said Thailand was stepping into the breach to compete with Brazil as a raws supplier to Black Sea customers -- traditionally unusual because of the geographical distance and freight rates involved.

But with Thailand-Black Sea rates at around $34 for smaller vessels, the total cost involved to put Thai cargoes into the region compared favourably with non-mechanically loaded Brazil cargoes, they said.

Other traders said demand was slackening for Brazilian raws, with more whites being quoted. Brazilian 45 ICUMSA cargoes were quoted at a discount of $10 to London futures and were getting even cheaper still.

"There's very little sugar actually being offered in the market. There isn't a great deal of demand...and I just think people are afraid to chuck too much sugar around the market with offers and bids," said one.
Another factor is the internal sugar price in Brazil, which traders said had fallen sharply of late. A lower internal price would normally lead to increased exports to the world market.
"It seems the domestic price in Brazil has fallen considerably. It has a tendency to do that at the beginning of the crop anyway," he said.
